question.text:
A 34-year-old woman, 4 weeks postpartum, comes to the clinic reporting hip tightness that occurs during prolonged sitting. During osteopathic structural examination, the following findings are noted:
- Right-sided positive seated flexion test
- Anterior motion detected when applying anterior force on the sacrum in prone position
- Deep sacral sulcus on the right side
- Posterior inferior lateral angle of the sacrum noted on the left
- L5 vertebra demonstrates left side-bending

What is the most accurate diagnosis?
Answer Choices: (A) Left on right anterior sacral rotation (B) Right on right posterior sacral torsion (C) Left on left anterior sacral torsion (D) Left sacral shear (E) Bilateral sacral extension dysfunction (F) Right on left posterior sacral torsion (G) Sacral counternutation dysfunction (H) Right unilateral sacral flexion (I) Left on left anterior sacral rotation (J) Bilateral sacral flexion dysfunction

options.A: Left on right anterior sacral rotation
options.B: Right on right posterior sacral torsion
options.C: Left on left anterior sacral torsion
options.F: Right on left posterior sacral torsion
options.I: Left on left anterior sacral rotation

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical findings point towards a left-sided anterior sacral rotation. The positive seated flexion test, anterior motion of the sacrum in prone position, and left-side bending of the L5 vertebra all suggest a left-sided rotation. The deep sacral sulcus on the right side is a compensatory finding.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The positive seated flexion test and anterior motion of the sacrum in prone position are key indicators of anterior sacral rotation.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other options are possible, the constellation of findings strongly favors left-sided anterior sacral rotation. Right-sided posterior sacral torsion (B) is less likely given the anterior motion. Left-sided anterior sacral torsion (C) is also possible, but the right-sided deep sulcus and L5 side-bending make left-sided rotation more probable. Sacral shear (D) is less likely given the specific rotation pattern. Bilateral sacral extension dysfunction (E) doesn't fully explain the specific findings. Sacral counternutation dysfunction (G) is not directly supported by the findings. Right unilateral sacral flexion (H) and Bilateral sacral flexion dysfunction (J) are less likely given the specific rotation pattern.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's right-sided positive seated flexion test, combined with the left posterior inferior lateral angle of the sacrum and left side-bending of L5, indicates right on left posterior sacral torsion. This torsion pattern explains the hip tightness during prolonged sitting and the specific findings on examination.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Right-sided positive seated flexion test with left posterior inferior lateral angle of the sacrum
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While sacral shear (D) and bilateral sacral flexion dysfunction (J) were considered, the unilateral nature of the findings and the specific pattern of motion (right flexion with left posterior angle) points more strongly to right on left posterior sacral torsion (F).

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The findings of right-sided positive seated flexion test, anterior motion on sacrum in prone, deep right sacral sulcus, and left posterior inferior lateral angle suggest right sacral base posterior rotation with left sacral base anterior rotation — consistent with right on right posterior sacral torsion. The L5 left side-bending supports this as a compensatory mechanism.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Right-sided positive seated flexion test and deep right sacral sulcus indicate right sacral base posterior rotation, which is the hallmark of right on right posterior sacral torsion.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Left on left anterior sacral torsion (C) and left sacral shear (D) were considered but contradicted by the right-sided findings. Bilateral or unilateral flexion (H, J) and counternutation (G) do not fit the specific rotational pattern observed.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: C, D, E, J (all bilateral or left-sided shear or flexion), G (counternutation, less likely given the test location and direction), H (unilateral flexion, but no clear support from the exam), I (left-sided rotation, contradicts the right-sided symptoms). The asymmetric test response and rotational maneuver make A the best fit.
